Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for acute deltoid ligament
injuries.
Perform an appropriate workup of deltoid ligament injuries.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of deltoid ligament injuries.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Pathomechanics
Injuries to the deltoid ligament commonly occur with a pronation mechanism of injury.
Rupture of the deep deltoid ligament renders the medial aspect of the ankle unstable.1
This rarely occurs without a concomitant injury to the lateral ankle ligament complex.




NOTES

A deltoid ligament injury also is commonly associated with a Maisonneuve injury, high ankle
sprain, or fibular fracture.
Anatomic reduction and fixation of the fracture and/or syndesmotic components often
ensures that the deltoid injury can heal on its own.2
Radiographic studies have suggested that the deltoid ligament is injured in 10% of patients
with an ankle fracture.3 Arthroscopic studies have shown that the deltoid ligament is injured
in approximately 40% of patients with an ankle fracture.4 In addition, as many as 65% of
isolated Weber type B distal fibula fractures are associated with an increase in the medial
clear space of more than 4 mm or valgus tilt on stress examination.5
In patients with chronic deltoid insufficiency, malalignment of the foot must be ruled out.
The most common deformity of the foot associated with a deltoid ligament injury is pes
planovalgus (flatfoot).
Overview
The medial ankle ligament complex is associated with a much lower incidence of injury
compared with the lateral ligament complex.
A paucity of objective data is available on medial ankle instability.
After an injury, patients with recurrent ankle instability that cannot be explained by the status
of the lateral ankle ligaments may have an injury to the medial ankle ligament complex.
Epidemiology
A study at West Point found the incidence of isolated medial ankle injuries to be 5.1% in 1,206
patients. The study also found that the injury was three times more likely to occur in men than
in women.6
Injuries to the deltoid ligament are commonly occur in combination with injuries to the lateral
ankle ligament complex or injuries to the syndesmosis.7
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The bracket-shaped socket of the ankle mortise contains the talus. The deltoid ligament on the
medial side is the main stabilizer to valgus stresses to the ankle joint.

9/3/26, 7:50 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156

The bony geometry of the ankle contributes to 100% of the translational stability and 60% of
the rotational stability of the ankle.8
The superficial layer of the deltoid ligament originates on the anterior colliculus and inserts on
the navicular, sustentaculum tali, and posteromedial tubercle of the talus8 (Figure 1).
The deep layer originates on the inferior and posterior colliculus of the medial malleolus and
inserts on the medial and posteromedial aspects of the talus.
Figure 1 Illustrations of ankles show deltoid ligament anatomy. A, The superficial deltoid
ligament consists of the superficial posterior tibiotalar ligament, the tibiocalcaneal ligament, the
tibiospring ligament, and the tibionavicular ligament. B, The deep deltoid ligament consists of the
deep posterior tibiotalar ligament and the deep anterior tibiotalar ligament. (Reproduced from
Lee S, Lin J, Hamid KS, Bohl DD: Deltoid ligament rupture in ankle fracture: Diagnosis and
management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2019;27[14]:e648-e658.)
Vascular Anatomy
The arterial supply most often originates from the medial tarsal artery and the tibialis
posterior artery. In a small number of patients, the arterial supply originates from the tibialis
anterior artery.9
A cadaver model study published in 2017 found that the deltoid has an intraosseous vascular
supply from the medial malleolus or the medial talus.9
Nerves Anatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
3/31

The saphenous nerve and vein often overlie portions of the deltoid ligament.
Tendons
The posterior tibial tendon runs along and superficial to the deltoid ligament. This tendon
serves as the primary dynamic stabilizer of the medial arch. Failure of the posterior tibial
tendon may increase stresses on the deltoid ligament and lead to chronic failure of the
ligament and the medial arch structures.10
Joints and Ligaments
The deltoid ligament can be divided into two main layers (Figure 2).
The superficial layer can be subdivided into three parts.
Tibiocalcaneal ligament
Tibiospring ligament
Tibionavicular ligament
The deep layer can be subdivided into two parts.
Deep posterior tibiotalar ligament
Deep anterior tibiotalar ligament
The superficial layer crosses the ankle and the subtalar joint, whereas the deep layer crosses
only the ankle.1
The anterior superficial deltoid is associated with rotatory stability.
The deep deltoid spans the tibiotalar joint and is the primary restraint to valgus tilt of the
ankle.11
Rupture of the deep and superficial deltoid is necessary for valgus tilting of the talus in the
ankle mortise.
The deep deltoid helps resist external rotation and lateral translation of the talus.
The deltoid ligament blends with the spring ligament distally before inserting on the navicular.
Concomitant injuries to the deltoid and spring ligaments are observed in patients with chronic
flatfoot deformity.12

Figure 2 Cadaver model photographs of the superficial (A) and deep (B) deltoid show the medial
ankle structures, including the deltoid ligaments and bony landmarks. Origin of superficial
posterior tibiotalar ligament (1), posteromedial talar tubercle (2), sustentaculum tali (3), spring
ligament (4), tuberosity of the navicular (5), talar neck (6), anterior malleolus (7), and distal center
of the intercollicular groove (8). (Reproduced from Lau BC, Barg A, Haytmanek CT, McCullough K,
Amendola A: Evolution in surgical management of ankle instability in athletes. J Am Acad Orthop
Surg 2021;29[1]:e5-e13.)
Etiology
Injuries to the deltoid ligament complex occur with internal rotation, pronation-eversion,
excessive plantar flexion, or excessive dorsiflexion forces.13
With a concomitant ankle fracture, the most common site of injury is an avulsion from the
tibial origin off the medial malleolus.14 A midsubstance tear also is common.
A lateral talar shift and an increased medial clear space of more than 4 mm is an indication of
an injury to the ligament.
Natural History
An acute rupture or chronic injury to the deltoid ligament leads to altered contact area and
peak pressures in the ankle mortise. The altered joint forces are thought to lead to ankle
arthritis.14
Valgus tilting of the talus in the ankle mortise often is observed in patients with chronic deltoid
injuries or severe acute injuries.
Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
5/31

In patients with a chronic flatfoot deformity or posterior tibial tendon insufficiency, the deltoid
is under altered stresses.12 These chronic altered forces on the medial structures of the foot
lead to increased forces on the deltoid ligament.
Subsequent valgus tilting of the talus within the ankle mortise is observed (Figure 3).
Figure 3 AP radiographs of an ankle with severe valgus. A, Preoperative radiograph
demonstrates severe valgus tilting of the talus within the ankle mortise secondary to a chronic
flatfoot deformity. Radiographs obtained 2.5 years (B) and 9.5 years (C) after deltoid ligament
reconstruction. (Reproduced with permission from Ellis SJ, Williams BR, Wagshul AD, Pavlov H,
Deland JT: Deltoid ligament reconstruction with peroneus longus autograft in flatfoot deformity.
Foot Ankle Int 2010;31[9]:781-789.)
Classification
Three classification systems are used for medial ankle sprains.
Hintermann classification15—a three-part classification system based on the location of the
tear in the deltoid ligament
Type I: tear or avulsion proximally off the tibia
Type II: tear in the middle of the superficial deltoid ligament
Type III: tear or avulsion distal and closer to the calcaneus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
6/31

American Medical Association standard nomenclature system16
Grade 1: ligament stretched
Grade 2: ligament partially torn
Grade 3: ligament completely torn
Beals classification17
Type I: rotational instability
Type II: rotational plus valgus instability
Mechanics of Injury
Tears more commonly affect the superficial deltoid ligament; however, severe tears also can
affect the deep deltoid.
The most common mechanism of injury is pronation or external rotation of the foot with
internal rotation of the tibia.
This injury can be observed in patients with sports injuries or in patients who twist their
ankles on uneven surfaces.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Sports in which deltoid ligament injuries commonly occur include basketball, soccer, rugby,
and gymnastics.
18
The most common mechanism of injury is an eversion or pronation force.
A feeling of the ankle giving way is commonly reported by patients with medial ankle
instability.
A truly acute, isolated deltoid ligament injury is rare.
Patients may report ankle instability; however, a feeling of instability is much less common
than in patients with injuries of the lateral ligament complex.19
Not uncommonly, patients also may note a history of lateral ankle instability.
A 2004 study by Hintermann et al20 showed that 75% of patients with chronic medial ankle
instability also had an avulsion of the anterior talofibular ligament. The inference was that a
loss of lateral ankle stability increases rotational instability of the ankle joint and, therefore,
increases stresses on the deltoid ligament.
Therefore, patients may report pain laterally, especially during dorsiflexion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
7/31

Patients may note prior medial ankle pain before the injury or a baseline flatfoot.
Medial tenderness, ecchymosis, and swelling are common on initial presentation.20
Stress examination is important and includes anterior/posterior, medial/lateral translation,
internal/external rotation, and varus/valgus stress tests (Figure 4).
Comparison of these examination findings with those of the contralateral, uninjured side is
important.19

Figure 4 Clinical photograph of a lower leg shows that manual external rotation stress
radiographs are obtained with the ankle in neutral dorsiflexion, the tibia internally rotated 10°,
and a manual external rotation force applied. (Reproduced from Aiyer AA, Zachwieja EC, Lawrie

CM, Kaplan JRM: Management of isolated lateral malleolus fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2019;27[2]:50-59.)
Physical Examination
The foot and ankle should be palpated along the medial and lateral borders. The most
common location for pain is along the medial gutter.19
Patients with medial ankle pain/instability also should be assessed for posterior tibial tendon
insufficiency.
The patient should be asked to stand, and the patient’s feet should be viewed from the front.
Any pronation of the longitudinal arch should be noted and compared with the contralateral
side.
The patient should then be viewed from behind. Any valgus of the hindfoot should be noted
and compared with the contralateral side.
The patient should be asked to perform a double- and single-stance heel rise to rule out
dysfunction of the posterior tibial tendon. If the patient can invert their hindfoot on heel rise,
posterior tibial tendon insufficiency is less likely.
The posterior tibial tendon also should be palpated for possible tenderness.
Because the spring ligament and the deltoid ligament blend into one another, chronic medial
ankle instability may lead to posterior tibial tendon insufficiency.
The clinical tests are similar to those for lateral ankle instability.
An inversion/adduction and eversion/abduction stress test should be performed and
compared with the contralateral ankle.
The examinations may need to be performed under anesthesia for a good assessment.
With the patient seated, the tibia is held in one hand, and the other hand is placed on the
lateral subtalar joint (including the talus) for the inversion stress test. The amount of
motion should be compared with that on the contralateral ankle. For the eversion stress
test, the tibia is held with one hand, and the medial subtalar joint is held with the other
hand and abducted. The amount of motion should be compared with that on the
contralateral side.
The anterior drawer test also can be used to determine medial instability.
Neurovascular Examination
Important to assess for traction injuries of the saphenous nerve

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing mortise and lateral radiographs commonly will not reveal a valgus ankle
deformity in an acute setting.
Chronic deltoid injuries, especially stage IV flatfoot deformity, will reveal valgus tilting of the
talus in the ankle mortise.

Radiography
Currently, dynamic imaging via stress radiography is standard practice for the detection
of tibiotalar instability.21 The gravity stress test can be performed to assess the deltoid
ligament (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Clinical photograph of a lower leg shows that gravity stress radiographs are
performed with the patient in the lateral decubitus position with the most distal half of
the affected leg over the table. A bump is placed under the calf, allowing the foot to fall
into external rotation. (Reproduced from Aiyer AA, Zachwieja EC, Lawrie CM, Kaplan JRM:
Management of isolated lateral malleolus fractures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2019;27[2]:50-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
11/31

59.)
The patient lies with his or her lateral side down to stress the medial soft-tissue
structures. The most distal half of the leg is then placed over the end of the table,
allowing the foot to fall into external rotation because of gravity. A standard mortise
radiograph of the ankle is then obtained.21
Michelson et al22 assessed the accuracy of the gravity stress test. In eight cadaver model
specimens, superficial and deep deltoid transection in combination with a fibular
osteotomy resulted in a lateral talar shift of 2 mm or more in all the specimens if the
gravity stress test was performed. This technique does not expose the physician to
irradiation and applies constant stress to the ankle, which is reproducible. In addition,
the position of the ankle does not alter the effectiveness of the examination.22 In a
prospective study of patients with an isolated supination–external rotation fibula
fracture, Schock et al23 clinically demonstrated that gravity stress radiographs are as
effective as manual stress radiographs but are less painful.
A manual external rotation stress radiograph can be obtained to assess for instability
(Figure 4). Manual external rotation stress radiographs are obtained by manually
internally rotating the tibia approximately 10° while externally rotating the foot with the
ankle in neutral dorsiflexion.21
Several studies have suggested that a medial clear space greater than 4 to 5 mm
indicates deltoid ligament disruption. Park et al24 obtained fluoroscopic mortise
radiographs of six cadaver model ankles after destabilizing the ankles according to the
supination–external rotation mechanism. The authors reported a sensitivity, specificity,
positive predictive value, and negative predictive value of 100% for absolute medial clear
space greater than 5 mm with applied dorsiflexion and external rotation. Clinically,
Schottel et al25 noted that a medial clear space cutoff value of greater than 5 mm
resulted in a sensitivity and specificity of 66% and 77%, respectively, for a deltoid
ligament tear confirmed via MRI. Using a medial clear space cutoff value of 4 mm, the
sensitivity was 73% and the specificity was 46%. Park et al24 reported an inherent
problem with stress imaging because of the amount of stress applied and because the
angle of the imaging affects the positive predictive value for deep deltoid injury.

Weight-bearing radiographs are beneficial to assess the competence of the deltoid
ligament.
Hoshino et al26 evaluated 38 patients with an isolated lateral malleolus fracture. The
patients returned to the clinic 7 days post injury and were evaluated via weight-bearing
radiographs. If the medial clear space was less than or equal to 4 mm, then the patients
continued nonsurgical treatment. If the medial clear space was greater than 4 mm, the
deltoid ligament was considered ruptured and the patient was offered surgical
treatment. Medial clear space widening was noted in 8% of the patients at follow-up;
these patients were offered surgical treatment. At a follow-up of 1 year, the mean
American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society score was 91 (± 8.1; good to excellent
results). These findings are consistent with those of Holmes et al.27 Patients with a
Weber type B ankle fracture and an intact mortise on initial non–weight-bearing
radiographs were seen at a follow-up of 1 week, at which time gravity stress radiographs
were obtained. Surgical treatment was recommended for patients with a medial clear
space greater than a cutoff value of 7 mm. Fifty-one patients without medial clear space
widening observed on gravity stress radiographs were followed for 1 year via serial
weight-bearing radiographs to evaluate for medial clear space widening. At final follow-
up, the mean American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society hindfoot score was 93.2. All
the patients except one had a decreased medial clear space at a follow-up of 1 year, and
clinical fracture union was 100%..27
Varus and valgus stress ankle radiographs should be obtained to confirm the
diagnosis and determine whether the deformity is fixed or dynamic (Figure 6).
The same stress examinations performed during the clinical assessment can be
performed radiographically for a more precise assessment of the injury. Anesthesia
may be necessary in patients with fresh or painful sprains.
An inversion/adduction and eversion/abduction stress test should be performed with
radiographs and compared with that of the contralateral ankle. The amount of
tibiotalar tilt should be measured. The normal range for varus tilt of the talus in the
ankle mortise is no eversion.28 No studies have been conducted to assess the
reliability of medial stress examinations.
A syndesmosis-specific stress examination is important to determine whether an
injury to the syndesmosis also is present.2

Figure 6 Stress radiographs of an ankle demonstrates medial instability with tilting,
lateral gapping indicating instability of the lateral ligaments (A), and medial gapping
indicating instability of the deltoid ligament (B). (Reproduced from Lau BC, Barg A,
Haytmanek CT, McCullough K, Amendola A: Evolution in surgical management of ankle
instability in athletes. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[1]:e5-e13.) 
Computed Tomography
CT may be beneficial in determining an avulsion of the ligament, which is commonly observed
from the tibia.7,15,20
Recently, weight-bearing CT scans have begun to be used to assess injuries and deformity of
the foot and ankle under physiologic weight. Currently, no studies have reported the use of
such imaging studies to assess acute injuries to the deltoid ligament.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the most common imaging modality used to assess an injury to the deltoid ligament29
(Figure 7).

The best MRIs for this purpose are T2-weighted images, and the best planes to view the injury
are the axial and coronal planes.29
MRI clearly shows degeneration or a tear in the deltoid ligament and other medial arch soft-
tissue structures.
Figure 7 MRIs of an ankle with multiple acute tears of the deep and superficial deltoid ligaments
from a twisting injury. A, Coronal T2-weighted fat-suppressed MRI shows a midsubstance tear of
the deep deltoid ligament (arrow). Bony edema is observed at the superficial deltoid ligament
origin (arrowheads). B, Axial proton density fat-suppressed MRI shows avulsion of the superficial
deltoid ligament from the medial malleolus (MM; arrow). Discontinuity of the deltoid ligament is
noted with the arrowhead. (Reproduced with permission from Crim J, Longenecker LG: MRI and
surgical findings in deltoid ligament tears. AJR Am J Roentgenol 2015;204[1]:W63-W69.)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

In a 2014 study, Nortunen et al30 reviewed the MRIs of 61 ankles with a deltoid ligament
injury. Radiographic findings of medial clear space widening were noted in 33 of the
ankles; radiographic findings of medial clear space widening were not noted in 28 of the
ankles. These findings suggested that MRI may not accurately predict deltoid injuries
that will require surgical management.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography may be used to confirm a deltoid ligament injury31 (Figures 8 and 9).

stress test. Clinical photographs show that measurements are obtained with the ankle in

with one hand while another hand touches the plantar aspect of the foot to control the

Ultrasonography
No studies have assessed the accuracy or utility of ultrasonography; however, as a
dynamic diagnostic imaging modality, it may be more effective than static diagnostic
modalities (eg, MRI) in assessing true medial instability.31
Arthroscopy
Arthroscopic assessment of the ligaments has been explored.32 Arthroscopy can be used for
assessment of articular reduction, management of osteochondral lesions, and lavage of
inflammatory cytokines.3

Arthroscopy
The deltoid ligament can be observed under direct visualization with the use of a small
joint arthroscope as the ankle is stressed or by using a probe to mobilize the tissue
directly at the medial malleolus attachment site.3
A drive-through sign also may be used arthroscopically to evaluate the deltoid ligament.3
This is done by attempting to pass the camera or the arthroscopic shaver through the
medial ankle gutter between the medial malleolus and the talus. In general, stable

9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
18/31

ankles with intact deltoid ligament fibers preclude successful drive-through this
anatomic plane.3
Differential Diagnosis
Medial talar body fracture
Medial malleolus fracture
Spring ligament injury
Posterior tibial tendon injury
Sustentaculum tali fracture
Management
For chronic injuries in patients genu valgum and pes planus, corrective surgical management
should include the restoration of proper limb alignment to remove the stresses on the deltoid
ligament.33
For acute injuries, direct ligament repair and ligament augmentation procedures have been
described.
The efficacy of one technique over another has not been scientifically evaluated.
Ankle fusion is a salvage procedure for the management of acute or chronic injuries if
management has been unsuccessful and degenerative changes of the ankle have occurred.
Nonsurgical Management
For deltoid ligament injuries in patients with a fibular fracture, with or without a syndesmotic
injury, selection of treatment may depend on the reducibility of the ankle mortise.
If the ankle mortise is stable after reduction of the fibular fracture and, if necessary, the
syndesmosis, then direct repair of the deltoid is not necessary;34 however, studies in progress
may demonstrate that acute deltoid injury requires repair via anatomic lateral column
reconstruction. This topic remains a subject of debate among experts.
In patients with a Hintermann type I or type II deltoid ligament injury, the use of a splint or
controlled ankle motion [CAM] boot for 1 to 2 weeks followed by functional rehabilitation is
recommended.34 For patients with a type III injury, immobilization for 3 to 4 weeks followed by
functional rehabilitation, including proprioception training, is recommended.35

9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
19/31

If the fibula and syndesmosis are fixed surgically, intraoperative fluoroscopy should be used to
assess the integrity of the deltoid ligament with the use of the stress tests already mentioned.
Indications
Isolated type I or type II deltoid ligament injuries commonly can be managed with the use of a
CAM boot for several weeks, followed by functional rehabilitation.
Contraindications
For acute injuries of any grade, surgical management is recommended if reduction of the
ankle mortise cannot be maintained.
Surgical Management
For non-posterior tibial tendon insufficiency or chronic injuries, direct repair of the deltoid
ligament is the most common technique.
In patients with posterior tibial tendon insufficiency, deltoid ligament reconstruction is an
option. Several techniques have been described in the literature.36-38
Direct repair of an isolated deltoid ligament injury is recommended in younger patients or
high-level athletes.
Indications
High-level athletes or younger patients
Injuries in which the ankle mortise cannot be reduced or reduction of the ankle cannot be
maintained
Contraindications
A stable ankle mortise
Low-demand patients or high-risk surgical candidates
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Deltoid Ligament Instability Disease
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001156
20/31

Planning should be based on a thorough patient history and physical examination.
Appropriate imaging studies and stress examination should be performed.
Thorough knowledge of the bony and relevant neurovascular structure is necessary.
Patient Positioning
A supine position without a hip bump (or with a hip bump on the contralateral extremity)
works well in patients with an isolated deltoid injury because it allows the leg to sit externally
rotated.
If the fibula or syndesmosis needs to be addressed, a hip bump can be used to internally
rotate the leg. In this situation, after the lateral structures of the ankle have been addressed,
the bump can be removed intraoperatively, allowing the leg to externally rotate, providing
good exposure to the medial side of the ankle and the deltoid ligament.
Surgical Approaches
Deltoid ligament repair
For an acute injury, direct repair with the use of suture anchors is recommended (Figure 10).
Intrasubstance repair normally is performed with the use of nonabsorbable suture.18
A vertical longitudinal incision travels 2 cm proximal to the medial malleolus toward the
sustentaculum tali. This will allow access to the superficial and deep deltoid ligament. The
need to make this incision along the anterior border of the medial malleolus toward the
navicular is a common misconception. The latter incision will not afford access to the deep
deltoid ligament (which is more posterior and deep to the posterior tibial tendon).
Dissection is performed down to the periosteum so the deltoid and, if necessary, the spring
ligaments can be identified. The posterior tibial tendon sheath should be opened, and the
tendon should be examined for any tears or degeneration. If a tear is present, it should be
directly repaired. The tendon should otherwise be protected throughout the procedure.
The saphenous nerve and vein often are located anterior to the incision. These structures
also should be protected.
The superficial deltoid ligament should be examined for tears or avulsions. To visualize the
deep deltoid, retract the posterior tibial tendon.
Immediate visualization of the deep deltoid may indicate a rupture or tear.
The origin of the superficial ligament on the medial malleolus is identified and debrided if
necessary. The origin of the ligament on the medial malleolus is then roughened, and a

Deltoid ligament reconstruction
A few techniques using allograft, autograft, or synthetic graft have been described.10,38-41
Reconstruction is more commonly used to manage deltoid ligament injuries in patients with
flatfoot deformities; however, reconstruction of the ligament occasionally is used to manage
deltoid failure in patients with a valgus ankle arthroplasty implant.38
A vertical longitudinal incision is made 2 cm proximal to the medial malleolus toward the
sustentaculum tali. This will allow access to the superficial and deep deltoid ligament. The
need to make this incision along the anterior border of the medial malleolus toward the
navicular is a common misconception. The latter incision will not allow access to the deep
deltoid ligament (which is more posterior and deep to the posterior tibial tendon). The
incision is made 1 cm proximal to the medial malleolus down to the navicular.
If a flexor digitorum longus transfer in combination with deltoid ligament reconstruction will
be necessary, the incision may curve distally toward the inferior navicular.
The saphenous nerve and vein often are located anterior to the incision. Next, the drill holes
for the graft are made in the tibia, talus, and calcaneus (Figure 11).
Drill holes mimic the insertion of the deep and superficial deltoid ligaments. These drill
holes traverse the talus 1 cm inferior and 1 cm posterior to the intercollicular groove and
from the sustentaculum tali are directed inferior and anterior to exit 1 cm proximal to the
calcaneocuboid joint.
A drill hole also is made at the origin of both ligaments. The most isometric spot is the
intercollicular groove at the tip of the medial malleolus.
After selection of the graft material (normally allograft), the graft is passed through the talus
drill hole and anchored on the opposite cortex with the use of a metallic button and then is
looped and passed through the tibial tunnel, exiting at the anterior tibia (1 cm of loop visible
through the exit point of the tunnel). It is then measured, sectioned, and passed through the
calcaneal tunnel and anchored on the opposite calcaneal cortex with the use of a metallic
button.

and-post construct. Because the deltoid ligament is largely vertical, maximal tension can be
performed without compromising ankle motion.

A well-padded splint should be used or 10 to 14 days postoperatively. The splint may be
removed for compression wrapping to minimize postoperative edema.
The ankle should be splinted in neutral. Alternatively, a CAM boot locked in neutral can be
used.
Passive range of motion can be initiated 7 to 14 days postoperatively (depending on associated
procedures). Patients should remain non–weight bearing for at least 3 to 4 more weeks
(depending on associated procedures). A CAM boot or a non–weight-bearing cast can be used.
Although data on clinical outcomes of deltoid ligament reconstruction are limited, most
patients remain non–weight bearing for 4 to 8 weeks postoperatively and then slowly progress
to full–weight bearing.
For at least 6 months postoperatively, patients should wear an ankle brace.
Complications
Pain
Stretching or compression of the saphenous nerve during retraction may cause paresthesias.
Under-tightening of deltoid repair or reconstruction may lead to a recurrent feeling of
instability or failed surgical management. Overtightening of this vertical ligament is difficult to
achieve but may lead to varus ankle alignment in patients with multidirectional instability.
Infection
Infection concerns are similar to those associated with all orthopaedic surgery procedures.
Fracture
Fracture of the medial malleolus or the talus can occur during preparation of the drill holes.
Hardware Failure
Repair sutures can attenuate if stresses are applied to the repair before the ligament heals.
Similarly, interference screws, if used, can pull out of the bone and may fracture the
sustentaculum tali given the smaller size of that structure.
Instability

Recurrent instability can occur, usually via failure of the construct.
Soft-Tissue Reaction
Suture abscesses can occur with absorbable sutures.
Stiffness
Overtightening of deltoid ligament repair rarely results in stiffness.
However, overtightening of deltoid ligament reconstruction may result in stiffness.
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Can use typical postoperative deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis, such as aspirin or a stronger
treatment option.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Care should be taken to identify and protect the saphenous nerve.
Outcomes
Hintermann et al20 presented a prospective case study of 52 arthroscopically repaired deltoid
ligaments. Good to excellent results were observed in 90% (46 ankles) at a mean follow-up of
4.4 years. Interestingly, 77% (40 ankles) also had lateral ligament instability.
Raikin and Myerson42 reported on nine patients who sustained an isolated medial ankle sprain
and underwent deltoid ligament repair. At a mean follow-up of 3.3 years, 77% (seven patients)
were able to return to their preinjury sporting activities.
A recent systematic review compared deltoid ligament repair, in patients with a concomitant
fibular fracture with management consisting of fixation of the fibular fracture only.43 At a
minimum follow-up of 12-month, three studies, which included 192 patients (81 who
underwent ligament repair; 111 who did not undergo ligament repair), met the inclusion
criteria. Patients who underwent deltoid ligament repair at the time of fixation of the fibular
fracture had better correction and maintenance of the medial clear space, better pain scores,
and similar complication rates compared with the patients who did not undergo ligament
repair; however, functional outcomes were similar between the two groups (Table 1).

Several techniques have been described for reconstruction of the deltoid ligament;10,37-40
however, few studies have reported patient outcomes.
Jeng et al40 reported results for eight patients with stage IV flatfoot deformity who
underwent minimally invasive deltoid ligament reconstruction. At 3 years postoperatively,
five of the eight patients maintained reduction of the tibiotalar joint and Medical Outcomes
Study 12-Item Short Form functional scores were equal to age-matched normative scores.
Ellis et al10 reported clinical outcomes for five patients who underwent deltoid ligament
reconstruction with the use of peroneus longus autograft. At 9 years postoperatively, all
patients maintained appropriate reduction of the tibiotalar joint and were satisfied with their
outcomes.
